tagline.text: A hat-shaped islet off Anilao with coral snorkeling

location.label: Location
location.text: Waters off Maricaban Island, Tingloy, Batangas (off Anilao)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (per person sharing the boat, entrance fee included)

children.text: Sombrero Island is a small uninhabited island off Anilao in Batangas that looks like a wide-brimmed hat from a distance. Its shallow coral reef is great for snorkeling, and it is only a 15–20 minute boat ride away, so it fits easily into an Anilao itinerary.

Sombrero Island is a small uninhabited island under the jurisdiction of Tingloy (Maricaban Island) in Batangas province. Its name comes from the word for "hat" in Spanish and Filipino, because the island rising abruptly from the sea is said to look like a giant upturned hat. Wikipedia lists it among the most visited beach attractions around Maricaban Island.

A shallow coral reef surrounds the island, and it is well known for snorkeling. One side has a small white-sand beach and the other a rocky shore, and many visitors report colorful coral even in shallow water about
3m
deep. It is also a famous dive site on the Anilao dive map, often called a "coral garden," so divers can explore the deeper parts while snorkelers enjoy the shallows.

Getting here is simple. Travel overland from Manila through Batangas City to Anilao Port, then hire a bangka boat. Many travelers add a half-day stop at Sombrero Island to an Anilao dive or resort stay. Boat prices and group sizes are negotiated on the day, so it helps to know the going rates beforehand.

The island is much better known than it used to be, so it gets crowded when several boats arrive, and many reviews mention a lack of toilets and showers. Some visitors also find the entrance fee and boat cost steep, so it is most rewarding if you are keen on swimming and snorkeling. If you only want to lie on a beach, nearby Masasa Beach or a resort beach is more comfortable.

The shallow reef around the island is full of coral and tropical fish, which makes snorkeling the most popular activity. One travel blogger described the water as literally crawling with life. An underwater camera or waterproof case is worth bringing. Please do not stand on or touch the coral; swim slowly at the surface to protect it.

The island is named for its shape, which resembles a wide-brimmed hat rising from the sea. The view as your boat approaches and the rocky scenery on the island are great for photos, and some visitors compare the rocks to an alien planet from a movie.

One side of the island has a short white-sand beach that is nice for resting after a swim. However, the sand is mixed with bleached coral fragments and pebbles that are uncomfortable on bare feet, so aqua shoes are needed.
Sombrero is one of the best-known dive sites in Anilao. The shallow coral garden lies at about
, while deeper slopes and walls continue at about
. You may meet turtles and rays. Currents can run on some days, so avoid going deep without a guide and follow the dive shop's briefing.
The opposite side of the beach is a rocky shoreline with balanced rocks here and there. Walking barefoot can cut your feet on sharp barnacles, so be careful.
From Gulugod Baboy, a mountain on the Anilao side, you can see Sombrero Island floating small on the sea. It pairs nicely with a visit to the island, before or after.
Sombrero is also a common stop on boat tours to Sepoc Island or Masasa Beach. Once you charter a boat, you can link several places in one trip.
At Anilao Port or your resort, settle the price, group size and timing with the boatman. The more people, the easier it is to split the boat cost.
Depart for Sombrero Island. The boat ride takes about
15–20 minutes
, longer if the waves are rough.
On arrival, pay the entrance fee (about
) and land. There is little shade, so rent a hut.
Put on a life jacket and snorkel gear, then snorkel over the coral. If you are not a strong swimmer, stay in the shallows.
Rest on the beach, take photos, and head back.

Going early means weaker sun and fewer boats, so it is much quieter. If the waves are too high to land, do not force it and postpone to another day. Divers can arrange a Sombrero dive through an Anilao dive shop.
Leave Manila by bus for the Batangas City Grand Terminal.
Take a jeepney to Anilao Port and find a boat.
Snorkel at Sombrero Island.
Eat a packed lunch or lunch ordered from your resort. The island only has a place that sells drinks.
Move on to the next stop such as Sepoc Island, or return to Anilao.
Head back, leaving plenty of time to catch a bus to Manila.
A day trip involves long travel and is tiring. If possible, stay a night in Anilao or Tingloy and enjoy it at a relaxed pace.
Take a bus from Manila (EDSA and other points) to the Batangas City Grand Terminal. It costs about
and takes
2–4 hours
. A bus signed CALABARZON is faster because it avoids the Lipa and Tanauan traffic.
At the Grand Terminal, transfer to a jeepney bound for Anilao. It costs about
and takes
40 minutes–1 hour
By car, take SLEX and then the STAR Tollway, exit at Batangas City, and head toward Mabini.
Bus and jeepney fares and travel times vary with traffic.
There is no scheduled passenger ferry to the island. Hire a bangka boat around Anilao Port or through your resort.
The boat ride takes about
15–20 minutes
. Boatmen usually carry up to 10 people, and some take up to 14 for an extra fee.
It is common to stop at Sombrero during a boat tour to Sepoc Island or Masasa Beach. The extra charge is often about
You can also ask the Mabini Tourism Office about boat availability.
Public boats to Tingloy leave several times a day from Anilao Port (or from Talaga Port during the rough habagat season). Fares reportedly rose to
regular as of April 2026.
You can also hire a boat on the Tingloy side to cross to Sombrero. The price is negotiated locally, and how it compares with a trip from Anilao is unconfirmed.
Public boats often leave only when full, and the last boat from Tingloy leaves early in the afternoon, so check the schedule locally.
The best time for Sombrero Island is November to May, when the sea is calm and clear. Visibility is good in this period, which makes snorkeling much more enjoyable.

Sea conditions depend heavily on the weather. In the rainy season from June to October, waves and swells grow, boat trips become difficult, and landing is sometimes impossible. One visitor wrote that afternoon waves made docking hard, so they stopped at Sombrero first.
Both Masasa and Anilao get crowded on weekends and holidays, so weekday mornings are the quietest. Around the full moon, currents get stronger for divers, so follow the advice of the local dive shop.

Overnight stays and tents are not allowed on the island, so you need to stay in Anilao or Tingloy. Anilao has many dive resorts, and Masasa and San Juan in Tingloy have homestay-type lodgings starting from about
per night. Prices vary by season, so confirm when you book.
The island has a hut that sells little more than drinks, and meals are often not sold. Order a packed lunch from your Anilao resort or bring your own, and always take your trash back with you.

Anilao has many divers, so seafood restaurants and resort restaurants are everywhere. Ordering Filipino dishes such as sinigang (sour soup), grilled fish and shrimp from your resort in advance makes a satisfying meal right after you return from the island. Homestays on the Tingloy side usually need meals requested separately, so let them know the day before.
Leave early for weaker sun and fewer people. Agree on the return time with the boatman beforehand.
Be sure to bring aqua shoes. The sand is mixed with coral fragments, and the rocky shore has sharp barnacles.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, a rash guard, sunscreen and plenty of water.
When hiring a boat, settle the group size, whether it is round trip, waiting time and stops first, then agree on the price.
The more people, the lower the cost per person. Boats usually carry up to 10 people.
An underwater camera or waterproof case helps you get good coral photos.
Bring plenty of cash in pesos. It is safest to assume cards and e-payments are hard to use on the island and on the boat.
Do not step on or touch the coral while snorkeling.
When looking for a boat in Anilao, it is safer to get a trustworthy boatman through resort staff or the Mabini Tourism Office.
Planning your return boat before 4 PM makes it easier to catch a bus to Manila from Anilao. Ask the boatman in advance whether late trips are possible.
The sea around the island is open and some spots have strong currents, so snorkel in a life jacket and give up landing on days with high waves.
Some reviews mention a strong undertow in certain areas. If you are not a confident swimmer, stay in the shallows and wear a life jacket.
The rocky shore has broken glass and sharp barnacles, so wear shoes.
Showers and toilets on the island are lacking or poor. Take care of that on the Anilao side if needed.
Overnight stays and tents are not allowed. Rules may change, so check the latest announcements.
It gets crowded on days when many boats arrive, and trips may be canceled in the rainy season, so check the weather.
The departure point for boats to Sombrero and the Philippines' leading dive area, with many resorts and dive shops.
A white-sand beach on Tingloy that can be combined with Sombrero for island hopping. The sunsets are beautiful.
A beach often combined with Sombrero on the same boat tour. An entrance fee is charged separately, and bookings go through Eagle Point Resort. It takes about

by boat from Anilao.
A diving and marine protected area off Batangas, best visited as a separate trip.
